title: Judge tosses drug trafficking convictions for B.C. compassion club founders
text:
Stated Claim / Post Context:
Judge tosses drug trafficking convictions for B.C. compassion club founders after constitutional challenge

A B.C. Supreme Court judge has ruled in favour of two harm reduction activists convicted of drug trafficking who argued they were doing it to reduce the harms caused by toxic drugs.

Actual Article Body:
The founders of a Vancouver-based compassion club that sold uncontaminated drugs to its members have had their drug trafficking convictions stayed after they successfully challenged the constitutionality of Canada's drug laws.

On Tuesday, a B.C. Supreme Court judge found the Drug User Liberation Front's compassion club reduced the harms associated with the toxic drug crisis and did not negatively impact the community or public safety.

Justice Catherine Murray found part of Canada's Controlled Drugs and Substances Act unconstitutional and stayed the convictions against Jeremy Kalicum and Eris Nyx, who co-founded DULF.

Kalicum and Nyx were found guilty last year of drug trafficking after Vancouver police raided the club in 2023.

"Mr. Kalicum and Ms. Nyx have borne the burden of bringing a successful constitutional challenge, thereby doing the public interest a service at considerable personal cost," Murray said.

In her decision, Murray said the founders' mission was to save lives by offering a safer supply of drugs. They bought drugs on the dark web, tested them to make sure they weren't contaminated, and sold them to members at cost.

Murray said in court on Tuesday that the pair "selflessly" put themselves to the side for the cause.

She noted thousands of people have died due to toxic drugs since the public health emergency was declared in B.C. in 2016.

"It is one of the worst public health emergencies in living memory," Murray said.

Tim Dickson, one of the lawyers representing Kalicum and Nyx, said the court had recognized that his clients were acting in the public interest, despite the personal risk.

“Today was a real vindication of the actions that they took in running the compassion club," he said.

Murray said Kalicum and Nyx's constitutional challenge focused on the lack of ability to obtain an exemption from prosecution for otherwise illegal activities under the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act (CDSA).

The DULF founders said there were no pathways through the relevant laws that would have permitted a "non-medicalized safer supply program," like the DULF compassion club, which they said is "urgently needed to address a public health crisis of epic proportions," according to Murray.

Kalicum and Nyx developed an operating plan in 2021 for the compassion club that included procuring heroin, cocaine and methamphetamine on the dark web, because sourcing from a licenced supplier "was not possible under the current regulatory framework."

"The program ran outside the medical system; no prescription or medical oversight was required," Murray said in her decision.

They would store the drugs in a safe, test them for fentanyl, benzodiazepines and other impurities, and label the tested drugs with information about their contents and health warnings, according to the decision.

Their plan included screening compassion club members to make sure they were over 18 years old and currently using illicit drugs.

DULF also worked with researchers to study how well the club worked.

DULF applied for an exemption to operate the compassion club in August 2021.

Health Canada responded in May 2022 that it intended to refuse DULF's request for an exemption because its method of acquiring drugs on the dark web was not a "viable option for advancing the objectives of the CDSA."

DULF replied to Health Canada that they did not want to procure drugs from the dark web, but there were no legal options for obtaining the drugs. The judge called it a "paradoxical situation."

Health Canada denied DULF's application for an exemption in July 2022.

According to the judge, DULF "started putting together" the compassion club in that same month. The B.C. minister of health supplied a storefront to DULF, at no cost, in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside and designated it as an overdose prevention site.
